items.title: Saline di Trapani protagoniste del podcast WWF Viaggio in Oasi
items.description:
Sono le Saline di Trapani, in Sicilia occidentale, le protagoniste dell'episodio di novembre del podcast WWF "Viaggio in Oasi"
The post Saline di Trap
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie Sono le Saline di Trapani, in Sicilia occidentale, le protagoniste dell’episodio di novembre del podcast WWF “Viaggio in Oasi”. Riserva Naturale da oltre 30 anni, fin dall’inizio affidata dalla Regione Siciliana in gestione al WWF Italia, le saline si caratterizzano per il felice connubio tra l’attività economica , quella della produzione del sale marino con metodi tradizionali, alla tutela della biodiversità. Podcast WWF Le vasche infatti , sono la dimora di moltissimi uccelli acquatici (circa 240 le specie censite) oltre che “casa” per una moltitudine di invertebrati e insetti. Ce ne parla Silvana Piacentino, direttrice della riserva, che annuncia l’imminente candidatura dell’area tra le Riserve MAB Unesco della Biosfera, ma ci racconta anche la storia della spatola Icaro. La riserva è stata teatro, proprio di recente, della prima nidificazione con successo dei fenicotteri non solo nell’area, ma in tutta la Sicilia occidentale. Un risultato che premia gli sforzi di conservazione da parte del WWF in questi anni, grazie ai quali da situazioni di degrado e di abbandono si è passati alla rinascita di un luogo divenuto unico dal punto di vista paesaggistico e area indispensabile per la tutela delle rotte migratorie. Viaggio in Oasi Ascolta il podcast WWF di novembre dedicato alle Saline di Trapani Ascolta il podcast 24 Luglio 2026 Fenicottero rosa, prima storica nidificazione nella Riserva Naturale delle Saline di Trapani Nati i primi tre piccoli nella Riserva Naturale Orientata gestita dal WWF Italia. È il primo sito riproduttivo della specie nella Sicilia occidentale

items.title: Mediterraneo: WWF e Guardia Costiera rinnovano l’alleanza per difendere biodiversità e legalità
items.description:
Firmato il nuovo accordo triennale per rafforzare la tutela delle specie marine, promuovere una pesca sostenibile e contrastare gli illeciti
The post
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie In un Mediterraneo sempre più minacciato dalla perdita di biodiversità, dall’inquinamento, dagli effetti del cambiamento climatico e dalla crescente pressione sulle risorse naturali, il Comando Generale delle Capitanerie di porto – Guardia Costiera e WWF Italia ETS hanno rinnovato la propria collaborazione firmando un nuovo accordo triennale per la tutela dell’ambiente marino e costiero. L’importanza della collaborazione L’intesa consolida una partnership ormai storica e punta a rafforzare le attività comuni per la conservazione della biodiversità, la promozione della sostenibilità delle attività marittime e della pesca, la diffusione della cultura della legalità ambientale e il coinvolgimento dei cittadini nella salvaguardia del patrimonio naturale del nostro Paese. Il Mediterraneo ospita una straordinaria ricchezza biologica ma è anche uno dei mari più sfruttati al mondo. Per affrontare queste sfide è necessario rafforzare la collaborazione tra istituzioni, comunità scientifica, organizzazioni della società civile e operatori del mare. Il nuovo accordo nasce proprio con questo obiettivo: mettere a sistema competenze, esperienze e capacità operative per trasformare la tutela del mare in azioni concrete e risultati misurabili. Le priorità della collaborazione Tra le priorità della collaborazione vi saranno la tutela delle specie marine più vulnerabili, il miglioramento dello stato di conservazione degli ecosistemi costieri e marini e la promozione di modelli di gestione sostenibile delle risorse ittiche. L’accordo prevede infatti attività congiunte di sensibilizzazione per la mitigazione delle catture accidentali delle specie protette, il rafforzamento dei percorsi di cogestione della piccola pesca e la sensibilizzazione degli operatori del settore, come pure l’attivazione di percorsi condivisi sul contrasto alla pesca illegale, non dichiarata e non regolamentata. Un ruolo centrale sarà inoltre svolto dalle attività di educazione ambientale, formazione e comunicazione rivolte a cittadini, scuole e comunità costiere, con l’obiettivo di promuovere una maggiore consapevolezza sull’importanza del mare per il benessere delle persone, l’economia e la resilienza dei territori ma anche per prevenire e contrastare le illegalità. La collaborazione valorizzerà anche le esperienze maturate dal WWF nella conservazione delle tartarughe marine, nella tutela delle specie costiere e nel contrasto ai crimini ambientali, integrandole con l’azione quotidianamente svolta dalla Guardia Costiera nella vigilanza, nel controllo e nella protezione dell’ambiente marino e costiero. “Un impegno comune” “La tutela del mare richiede alleanze solide e una visione condivisa. Il rinnovo di questo accordo conferma l’impegno comune nel difendere il patrimonio naturale del Mediterraneo e costruire un futuro in cui conservazione della biodiversità, attività economiche sostenibili e benessere delle comunità costiere possano procedere insieme. In un momento storico in cui il mare affronta pressioni senza precedenti, rafforzare la collaborazione tra istituzioni e organizzazioni della società civile è una scelta tanto necessaria quanto strategica”, ha dichiarato il presidente del WWF Italia Luciano Di Tizio. “La tutela dell’ambiente marino rappresenta una delle missioni prioritarie della Guardia Costiera, che vi provvede quotidianamente attraverso attività di vigilanza, controllo e contrasto agli illeciti lungo le coste e in mare. Il rinnovo di questo accordo rafforza una collaborazione con il WWF che, negli anni, ha contribuito concretamente alla salvaguardia degli ecosistemi marini e alla diffusione della cultura della sostenibilità e della legalità ambientale. La condivisione di competenze ed esperienze rappresenta un valore aggiunto per tutelare le specie protette, promuovere una pesca più sostenibile e contrastare gli illeciti, sensibilizzando al contempo cittadini, scuole e operatori del settore sull’importanza della protezione del nostro patrimonio marino”, ha dichiarato il Comandante Generale del Corpo delle Capitanerie di porto – Guardia Costiera, Ammiraglio Ispettore Capo (CP) Pil. Sergio Liardo. L’accordo avrà una durata di tre anni e consentirà di sviluppare iniziative e progettualità congiunte a livello nazionale e locale, contribuendo al raggiungimento degli obiettivi di tutela della biodiversità marina, gestione sostenibile delle risorse e rafforzamento della partecipazione dei cittadini nella conservazione del mare. 15 Luglio 2021 10 cose da sapere su squali e razze Scopri le 10 principali curiosità su queste specie simbolo degli oceani Lucio Biancatelli 6 Giugno 2018 Accordo WWF Guardia costiera per la tutela del mare Il Comandante Generale del Corpo delle Capitanerie di Porto-Guardia Costiera, Ammiraglio Ispettore Capo Giovanni Pettorino e la Presidente del WWF Italia, Donatella Bianchi, hanno siglato oggi un Protocollo d’intesa fra il Comando Generale e l’associazione, che recentemente ha… Lucio Biancatelli 21 Settembre 2018 Al salone nautico di Genova tutti i numeri del tour WWF Spiagge plastic free Negli oltre 700 sacchi raccolti il ‘primato’ dei rifiuti è sempre la plastica “usa e getta”. L’evento conclusivo della Campagna #GenerAzioneMare ha lanciato WWF S.U.B una  nuova realtà di volontariato per ripulire i fondali #plasticfree #generazionemare  È stata una… Giulia Ciarlariello 3 Settembre 2020 69 tartarughine scoprono la vita in mare ad Agrigento Sabato 29 agosto gli operatori del Progetto tartarughe e del Life Euroturtles del WWF Gino Galia e Giuseppe Mazzotta hanno ispezionato e contato tutte le uova trovate in un nido di tartaruga marina scoperto nella spiaggia di Cannatello,…

Data centres are among the world’s fastest growing electricity consumers. An analysis of more than 9,000 facilities worldwide links the artificial intelligence-era expansion of data centres to delayed coal plant retirements and around 2 Gt of additional carbon dioxide emissions.

                        10 November 2026

Mongolia’s iconic grasslands are in crisis — invisible fungi could help save them

Clues suggest that underground fungal networks might be key to reviving degraded land and preserving plant biodiversity.
                
            
        
        
            
                
                    By

April Reese0

April Reese
                
                
                    
                        
                            April Reese is a journalist in Aveiro, Portugal.

More than 70% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, which has implications for the country’s nomadic herders.Credit: Timothy Allen/GettyRising temperatures, desertification and overgrazing are taking a heavy toll on Mongolia’s iconic desert grasslands, as well as its nomadic herding culture. But a team of researchers might have hit on an underground solution. They’ve found clues that protecting key fungal networks that support life above the surface could help to preserve biodiversity, boost climate resilience and revive degraded lands.In most ecosystems, invisible networks of fungi trade resources with plants by interlocking with their roots. These arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi provide the plants with nitrogen and phosphorus gathered from the soil; in return, the plants send excess carbon through their roots to the fungi, helping to sequester it from the atmosphere.“Mongolia has very unique fungal networks that power these arid grasslands,” says evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers at the Free University of Amsterdam. Kiers is leading a project to map and identify mycorrhizal-fungus hotspots in Mongolia. “As we fight desertification, we want to be able to protect the fungi that are going to be so important for these plants and ecosystems to be restored.”Working out ways to maintain healthy fungal networks cannot come quickly enough. Around 77% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, and the country is warming three times faster than the global average. Kiers says that paying more attention to fungal networks could help to address the interconnected global challenges of desertification, biodiversity loss and climate change.It seems that fungi might be starting to get the attention they deserve: last month, at the latest meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, held in Yerevan, Armenia, 3 more countries signed a pledge to conserve fungi, bringing the total number of signatories to 17. And a road map to help countries make good on that pledge, the Global Strategy for Fungal Conservation, was launched.Fungus mappingKiers’s team is part of the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), a non-profit organization that maps fungal systems around the world and works to protect them. Kiers co-founded the organization in 2021. In September, its researchers announced that they had found more than 500 types of fungus in southwestern Mongolia, 90% of which were previously unknown.Kiers’s team is in talks with several governments to present its maps of fungal hotspots and data in hopes of supporting the development of strategies to curb desertification and boost climate resilience.But at the same time as researchers such as Kiers are documenting fungal hotspots, the hotspots might be disappearing. In Mongolia, the team found that degraded land had at least 44% fewer species of mycorrhizal fungi and 60% less plant cover than did non-degraded land.

items.title: Transdisciplinary spaces for co-production: facilitating climate action in smaller municipalities through creating transformation knowledge
items.body:

Transdisciplinary spaces for co-production: facilitating climate action in smaller municipalities through creating transformation knowledge
                        Luise Spieker 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0003-6594-40531 & Birte Frommer2

npj Climate Action
                            volume 5,  Article number: 98 (2026) Cite this article
                        
                        
                            
    
        
            
                
                
                
                    
                    Save article
                
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

AbstractSmaller municipalities face numerous challenges in pursuing climate action, including the modernization of public buildings. Since buildings account for around 30% of CO2 emissions, they offer significant leverage. Structural barriers like limited funding and a lack of qualified personnel often hinder implementation – even when awareness, political will, and clarity on potential measures exist. This highlights that systems knowledge (facts) and target knowledge (norms and values) are insufficient without transformation knowledge (action-oriented knowledge). This article explores how small municipalities can develop transformation knowledge through co-production processes. Using a longitudinal study, we demonstrate the importance of trusted spaces for open dialog and scientific support to translate ideas into practical solutions. Transdisciplinary approaches, such as the three-phase model, are shown to effectively empower municipalities. By collaboratively developing tailored solutions, municipalities can overcome barriers and engage in impactful climate action, as demonstrated in a case study of municipalities in the German state of Hesse.

                        Climate change
                
            
                
                    
                        Social sciences

IntroductionThis paper focuses on climate action in local authorities as one important type of governmental action described by Tosun in her editorial to this journal1. Despite widespread engagement in climate protection across German municipalities, a recent study by the Federal Environment Agency reveals significant variability in the implementation of measures across different sectors. Notably, progress in energy modernization of municipal building stock remains far below expectations and requirements2. Given that buildings account for approximately 30% of CO2 emissions, improving energy efficiency in this sector represents a crucial leverage point for meeting climate targets3,4,5. However, even when municipalities recognize the urgency of climate action, demonstrate political will, and identify effective strategies such as building modernization, various structural barriers, e.g., limited financial resources and a lack of qualified personnel, frequently impede implementation6. These challenges are particularly pronounced in small municipalities, which often manage a large building stock of non-residential structures such as schools, kindergartens, and community centers. These buildings are frequently old, energy-inefficient, and subject to additional constraints such as monument protection regulations, further complicating modernization efforts. In particular, smaller municipalities play a vital role in advancing climate protection, as they represent a large share of the population (approximately 46% of Germans live in towns and municipalities with fewer than 50,000 inhabitants7). This constellation of challenges illustrates that systems knowledge (as fact-oriented knowledge) and target knowledge (as value-oriented knowledge) alone are not enough to achieve implementation8. Therefore, this article explores how municipalities, particularly smaller ones, can succeed in developing transformation knowledge (as action-oriented knowledge) to complement and operationalize existing knowledge types.A key focus is on building modernization, as it represents a critical area where transformation knowledge can help overcome structural and regulatory barriers, enabling municipalities to improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions in their extensive building stock. We examine which spaces are conducive to generating transformation knowledge and how smaller municipalities can be empowered to engage in climate action through co-production procedures despite their financial and personal challenges. By co-production, we refer – following Wyborn et al. – to iterative, collaborative processes involving practitioners and researchers to jointly frame problems, generate knowledge, and develop actionable solutions. This approach goes beyond knowledge transfer, aiming instead to integrate diverse forms of expertise into context-sensitive solutions9. We argue that transdisciplinary approaches, particularly the three phase-model, are well-suited to jointly work, test, and reflect on solutions and on transformation knowledge. Based on a longitudinal study, we demonstrate that creating a trusted environment for open exchange about challenges and frustrations within municipalities is essential. Equally important is the support of scientific experts who can help translate emerging ideas into practical solutions and facilitate the co-production of transformation knowledge10,11. We hypothesize that innovative spaces – defined as trusted environments outside of routine administrative settings that enable sustained peer exchange and scientific collaboration – significantly enhance the co-production of transformation knowledge and thus empower local authorities to implement climate action more effectively.This study draws on insights gained from a research project funded by the Hessian Ministry for Economic Affairs, Energy, Transport, Housing and Rural Areas (hereafter: funding ministry), focusing on the “Governance of Building Modernization in Small and Medium-Sized Municipalities in Hesse.” The project was limited to municipalities in Hesse in line with the funding ministry’s interest in a Hessian case study. Municipalities were selected based on specific criteria to ensure alignment with the research goals and to reflect the diversity of local contexts across Hesse, including both rural and urban settings with varying administrative and structural conditions. A key prerequisite for participation was the explicit willingness of the municipalities to engage actively in the project. All participating municipalities are members of the Hessian Climate Municipalities network, an initiative supporting local climate action. These municipalities were already implementing measures in the building sector at the time of the study. They also met several additional criteria: they employed a dedicated climate manager within their administration, and they had financial resources allocated for building modernization in their municipal budgets. Given these characteristics, we assume that the participating municipalities possessed a baseline level of systems knowledge (i.e., understanding the status quo of climate challenges affecting the local level) and target knowledge (i.e., clear climate action goals). This knowledge was embedded both within their administrative structures and their political decision-making processes. The study therefore focuses on how these municipalities, with their existing capacities, could develop transformation knowledge – practical, action-oriented strategies to overcome barriers and accelerate climate-friendly building modernization. Transformation knowledge is vital in this context because it avoids the common discrepancies between what the sciences know and what is the reality for municipalities. Our study therefore investigates how co-production processes – when embedded in transdisciplinary formats – can foster transformation knowledge that is both scientifically grounded and locally feasible.To further knowledge creation that is not only done by scientific agents but also (or especially by) municipal agents, it is vital to work transdisciplinary12. Axelsson et al. underscore that transdisciplinary research aims at solving real-world problems where cooperation between academic and non-academic actors is prerequisite13. Lang et al. describe transdisciplinarity as a “reflexive, integrative, method-driven scientific principle aiming at the solution or transition of societal problems and concurrently of related scientific problems by differentiating and integrating knowledge from various scientific and societal bodies of knowledge”14. This means that transdisciplinarity is characterized by reciprocal joint learning processes among researchers of different disciplines and practitioners. The term ‘practitioner’ is used in this paper as defined by Martin as a “catch-all phrase covering policy-makers (officials and politicians), managers and frontline public servants,” reflecting the range of municipal actors involved in climate action and co-production processes15.With reference to Jahn and Pohl and Hirsch Hadorn, Lang et al. describe the ideal transdisciplinary research process as having three phases14,16,17:Phase A: The first phase is dedicated to the joint formulation of the problem. In addition to describing the real-world problem and naming the research questions to be addressed jointly, the methodological approach in the project is defined here, and measures are taken to form the transdisciplinary team of researchers and practitioners18.Phase B is dedicated to the joint development of solutions for the previously formulated real-world problem. In this phase, the actual research takes place in co-creation between the scientists and the practitioners. It is important here to define exactly which service is expected from which actor.In Phase C, the solutions developed in Phase B are then implemented and used. Unlike other forms of knowledge transfer, where external expert reports are prepared and handed over to the client for implementation, the clients here have been actively involved in the solution development process during Phase B. This ideally results in a better fit of the solutions and greater commitment to their implementation14.More recent approaches differentiate these phases into further sub-phases such as phase A0 dedicated for initiating encounters between the relevant actors, A1 as a joint problem framing and visioning phase, A2 as the phase for generating specific ideas for change and agreeing on transfer questions, B1 for developing an B2 for testing solutions (see figure 1)19,20.These phases establish a transdisciplinary approach to creating knowledge. By including all agents throughout all of the phases and co-creating solutions to real-life problems, there is an increasing sense of ownership felt by the practitioners involved in the project. Lang et al. speak of “enhanced decision-making capacity of the practice actors”14.An inherent part of transdisciplinary research is the concept of co-production21,22,23. The term co-production is used in various scientific disciplines such as science and technology studies (STS), environmental sciences, health science and sustainability science. For the latter in particular, the co-production of solution options for sustainability issues is an important aspect in the realm of transdisciplinary projects and is therefore key in Phase B of transdisciplinary projects8,9,14,24. Based on an extensive literature review, Bandola-Gill et al. conceptualized the term co-production as a suitable approach to address complex (sustainability) problems24. Regardless of the respective key discipline, it is equally assumed that co-production requires the interaction of researchers and non-academic actors and that different intensities can be identified here. Analogous to Sherry Arnstein’s “Ladder of Citizen Participation” from 1969, various authors describe the degree of co-production on a scale from low to intensive co-production with stages ranging from information to consultation to collaboration to empowerment15,24,25,26. The study by Brandt et al. is particularly relevant here: in 104 of the case studies examined, the highest level of co-production, empowerment, was achieved only infrequently26. This finding leads Bandola-Gill et al. to conclude that this desirable level of co-production is not achieved as often as it could or should be24. Furthermore, co-production in general remains a relatively new and rarely utilized approach at the municipal level in Germany, despite its significant potential to drive innovation27.In addition to the concept of co-production, transdisciplinary research involves three key forms of knowledge: systems knowledge, target knowledge, and transformation knowledge. These concepts outline the roles of science in sustainable development, emphasizing its contribution as a provider of these knowledge types28,29 However, knowledge is not exclusive to the sciences. A fundamental principle of transdisciplinary research is recognizing that practitioners and individuals with real-world experience also hold essential insights crucial for achieving sustainable development.Systems knowledge encompasses existing insights into the current state of affairs and the historical processes that led to it30. This knowledge is crucial for identifying the problems that need to be addressed. Systems knowledge not only provides a comprehensive assessment of the status quo but also serves as a critical foundation for generating other types of knowledge necessary for progress17. In the context of this study, the practitioners involved - such as climate managers, building control department personnel, and, in some cases, mayors - bring extensive expertise in their respective fields. Their technical understanding of climate-friendly or climate-adapted modernization is particularly valuable. These experts are skilled in evaluating buildings and determining appropriate modernization strategies, always maintaining a practical focus on the current situation and its shortcomings.Target knowledge pertains to the objectives of a process: identifying the goals, determining the desired direction, and articulating these aims clearly to others. It involves forward-looking efforts to guide the way forward by evaluating existing system knowledge and developing visions or projections for the desired outcomes17,29. Related to this study, target knowledge focuses on the municipalities’ vision for modernizing their own buildings to make them more climate-friendly.Transformation knowledge is concerned with how to modify existing practices and introduce new ones to further the transformation in the chosen field of study or work. Following Horcea-Milcu et al., transformation knowledge can be understood “as knowledge about how to intervene (interventions, processes, pathways, and levers), and where to intervene (leverage points)“8. This knowledge identifies pathways for enacting change, whether through technical, social, legal, or cultural approaches28. Transformation knowledge is a key element in furthering sustainable development because solely posing the knowledge about how to modernize buildings to decrease carbon emissions is not enough to actually facilitate change. Equally important is determining the methods and strategies to reach these goals. By working together in a transdisciplinary project, both scientific insights and practical, real-world knowledge can be leveraged to develop actionable steps toward creating climate-friendly municipalities.These forms of knowledge are interdependent in the process of transdisciplinary research31. For example, target knowledge cannot exist without a solid understanding of the status quo – such as the current state of building modernization (systems knowledge). Only by thoroughly analyzing existing conditions can appropriate objectives and potential challenges in building modernization be identified. The same applies to transformation knowledge. Without a base in both systems knowledge (understanding the current state) and target knowledge (desired outcomes), it is impossible to develop effective strategies for transforming existing structures and promoting climate-friendly buildings in smaller municipalities.This paper demonstrates, in the following results and discussion sections, how transdisciplinary projects can facilitate the development of solutions to challenges in building modernization by co-producing transformation knowledge within thoughtfully designed spaces. These spaces, intentionally distinct from municipalities’ daily routines, provide a trusting environment where practitioners can step away from their everyday pressures to collaborate meaningfully with like-minded individuals. Over time, such environments foster open dialog, creativity, and problem-solving, ultimately enabling the production and implementation of transformation knowledge at the local level. This aligns with our central hypothesis: spaces that offer a trusting environment away from daily work routines, combined with opportunities for sustained exchange with like-minded people, can significantly enhance the generation of transformation knowledge and its practical application.However, such spaces are rarely available within standard government structures. They need to be deliberately created and supported by external agents, such as scientists and civic actors, who can facilitate the co-production process. An essential principle of transdisciplinary research is recognizing that valuable knowledge already resides within local practitioners17. Harnessing this expertise while integrating external perspectives is critical to crafting actionable solutions tailored to local challenges. We propose that transdisciplinary projects that establish these dedicated spaces are essential to addressing the complex barriers municipalities face and to producing the knowledge necessary for effective climate action.Existing studies often focus narrowly on the technical and policy instruments available for addressing climate challenges, such as municipal climate action plans, building efficiency standards, or funding schemes for renewable energy and retrofitting5,32,33. While such tools are important, this approach tends to overlook the social problems practitioners face and fails to account for the underlying administrative processes within municipalities that significantly affect implementation. By addressing these gaps, our study highlights how transdisciplinary approaches – and the creation of dedicated, trust-building spaces – can bridge this divide and foster actionable, context-sensitive solutions for local governments.ResultsThe results of the project unfold across four interrelated dimensions (see Fig. 1 for overview and typology). First, the project produced a set of co-produced, practice-oriented tools that support municipalities in navigating the complex governance of energy-efficient building modernization. Second, it fostered capacity building and empowerment among municipal staff, strengthening their ability to act and make informed decisions. Third, it established lasting collaborative structures and informal support networks that extended beyond the formal project context. Fourth and finally, the project enabled a feedback loop to the funding ministry, providing practical insights from the municipal level into policy-making. These four dimensions together reflect the project’s comprehensive approach to enabling transformation through transdisciplinary collaboration and knowledge co-production. The results presented below draw on the project’s outputs and activities as well as on findings from the project evaluation, including a standardized survey and subsequent interviews with participating municipal representatives.Fig. 1Full size imageOverview and typology of project results in four categories.Co-produced tools and tangible outputsAs part of the project, the participating municipalities developed several outputs with the project team that will help them in the future and could also be useful for other municipalities in similar situations. One of the key outputs is a governance profile for energy-efficient building modernization, developed for each municipality. This profile provides an overview of the current state of the municipal building stock, as well as the measures already implemented and planned for energy-efficient modernization in the respective municipality. These profiles range in length from 10 to 15 pages and are formatted as PDF files to ensure accessibility and ease of use (accessible via https://www.schader-stiftung.de/themen/stadtentwicklung-und-wohnen/fokus/governance-der-gebaeudemodernisierung/artikel/governance-der-gebaeudemodernisierung-kommunale-steckbriefe). Each profile includes images from the municipalities, adding a local and personalized touch to the content, ensuring the profiles are not only informative but also visually appealing. Co-produced through intensive collaboration between the municipality and the project team, the profiles are tailored specifically to the needs of each municipality. These governance profiles serve as a valuable tool for communication within the administration and political bodies. By summarizing the current state of building modernization efforts, they ensure that knowledge is not only retained in the minds of staff members but is also documented and made accessible. During the project, municipalities had sufficient time to systematically document and structure their knowledge of energy modernization processes. In doing so, these profiles not only provide crucial insight for the municipalities themselves but also serve as helpful references for other municipalities facing similar challenges.Of particular interest are the results deriving from the working groups Funding and Communication within the project. The thematic focus of these groups was chosen by the participants themselves, underscoring how the challenges in building modernization in municipalities often derive from governance issues instead of technical ones34. The Funding working group produced a practical guide to navigating Germany’s complex funding landscape (available via https://www.iwu.de/fileadmin/publikationen/handlungslogiken/KommGebGov/2025-04_Handreichung-F%C3%B6rderprozess.pdf). The main output was a detailed process flow chart illustrating the sequential steps of the entire building modernization process, designed to support municipalities in acquiring funding and managing the building modernization process. Unlike standard funding guidelines from state authorities or other advisory service providers, this presentation goes far beyond the pure funding process. It begins with an overview of the municipal building stock and its condition, providing a structured approach to the various stages of modernization. The flow chart outlines where and how funding opportunities can be applied throughout the process, from initial assessment to project completion. The flow chart is accompanied by explanatory notes that clarify each step and provide actionable insights. The combination of visual and textual elements ensures that users can quickly understand the process while having detailed information readily available for reference. Additionally, it offers valuable, practice-oriented tips on crucial points in the process that require special attention. Serving as an essential tool for orientation, the flow chart helps municipalities understand their current position within the overall modernization process, enabling them to navigate the complexities of building modernization more effectively and apply funding in an efficient and targeted way.Meanwhile, the Communication working group focused on devising strategies to effectively leverage municipal processes to advance building modernization goals. The main output was a document outlining communication channels that ensures political security and provides the administration with a clear framework for action (accessible via https://www.iwu.de/fileadmin/publikationen/handlungslogiken/KommGebGov/2025-05_Handreichung-Kommunikation.pdf). This document takes the form of a graphical representation of administrative practices, illustrating the various pathways that can lead to a political decision, as well as alternative routes for placing and promoting a topic within the municipality’s administration and political bodies, such as reports to political committees for information, formal requests, or proposals for decisions. For the participating municipalities, this visual tool highlights where specific documents or information can be introduced and which coordination processes can be followed at various stages. In doing so, it offers empowerment and support for administrative staff in implementing building modernization projects and a means of reflecting on experiences and lessons learned on what is working well or where more time or resources need to be allocated.The project also provided time for testing these solutions and a trial period to assess how they functioned within the administrative environment. This was particularly evident in the context of comprehensive modernization projects where the building modernization flow chart was successfully applied. The pilot projects included partial demolition and new construction, such as a sports facility, a kindergarten, and a municipal administrative site, demonstrating the effectiveness of the flow chart in guiding these complex processes.The graphical representation of administrative practices, which illustrates the various pathways for communicating and deciding municipal topics, was also tested in practical scenarios. These included the data collection for evaluating the current condition of municipal buildings, the preparation of an informational resolution for the municipal council, and the development of a fundamental resolution on the energy-efficient modernization of municipal buildings.During the whole co-production phase, the project team was also supportive in writing reports and resolutions if one of the participating municipalities got in touch and asked for help or feedback.Capacity building and empowermentRegarding empowerment and capacity building, the project created conditions for a trusting atmosphere between the participating municipalities and the project team. We established a space where participants felt comfortable sharing not only their challenges but also their successes and insights with others. This trust was fostered by explicitly defining the workshops as safer spaces where information would not be shared externally without consent, adhering to the Chatham House Rule35. These efforts complemented one another: the definition of workshops as safe spaces, the team’s consistent practice of active listening, and the ongoing availability between sessions together fostered an atmosphere of openness and trust. By actively listening, taking municipal agents’ contributions seriously, and valuing their input, the project team cultivated an environment in which participants felt encouraged to share openly. In this context, active listening – understood as an attentive and mindful way of engaging with others, rather than merely waiting for one’s turn to speak – is a key principle in transdisciplinary research36. Furthermore, the project team remained accessible between workshop sessions, offering support via phone calls or video meetings, whether to provide advice, listen to concerns, or connect participants with others who could offer assistance.The participants made frequent use of these opportunities throughout the project. They occasionally shared information that could benefit others or showcased progress in their respective municipalities. The project team then distributed these emails and documents to all participants, fostering a sense of collective learning. The project evaluation provided further insights into the value of this exchange. Interviewees, including participants with many years of professional experience in municipal administration, described discussions with colleagues from other municipalities as repeatedly valuable for reflecting on their own experiences and gaining new perspectives. Additionally, members of the project team visited several municipalities to gain a deeper understanding of the participants’ contexts and to strengthen their commitment to the project. This personal engagement had a positive impact on the participation levels of the municipalities visited. The interviews also highlighted the importance of the protected setting in enabling such open exchange. One participant contrasted the openness within the project with the reluctance to share information across municipalities outside this setting. The relevance of peer exchange became particularly apparent in challenging situations: one participant described how an unexpected political inquiry initially caused severe uncertainty, while the exchange and advice of colleagues helped him respond to the situation and was experienced as a formative moment.Sustained interaction and community buildingThe project’s approach to fostering collaboration among municipal actors aligns closely with the concept of a ‘community of practice’ which refers to a group of people who share a concern, set of problems, or passion about a topic, and deepen their knowledge and expertise through ongoing interaction37,38,39. From the outset, the project created conditions that enabled this type of informal and practice-based learning: through repeated exchanges, mutual support, and peer learning opportunities, municipal representatives gradually built trust and a sense of shared purpose. These connections extended beyond the formal workshop setting. Participants continued to share questions, challenges, and ideas with the project team via email or phone calls. More importantly, they also maintained ongoing communication among themselves, helping one another or initiating follow-up meetings to tackle pressing issues. This self-sustained collaboration exemplifies how a community of practice can emerge from structured but open-ended transdisciplinary engagement – and how such networks can continue to support municipal transformation processes after a project’s official end. Interview findings also shed light on how these interactions developed and were experienced by participants. Interviewees described this exchange with colleagues from other municipalities as particularly valuable for reflecting on their own experiences and learning from similar challenges. One participant summarized a key experience as realizing that ‘we are not alone’, as municipalities faced similar challenges despite differences in scale and context. At the same time, interviewees pointed to limitations to such open exchange beyond the protected project setting. They described a reluctance to share information across municipalities outside the project and expressed a wish for more opportunities for continued exchange.The presented results have been developed within the confidential framework of the project, respecting the careful and secure handling of partly sensitive information. Some insights highlighted here have been thoughtfully drawn from e-mail exchanges and confidential conversations, which honor the privacy and trust of the participants.Policy feedback and system effectsIn addition to identifying ways to support smaller municipalities in their governance of building modernization, the project maintained a structured feedback loop with the funding ministry. This included an interim report, a mid-term consultation, and a draft final report shared for feedback before formal submission. The ministry was also represented at both the kick-off and final events, which provided opportunities to reflect on challenges and insights from the field. At the final event, the Hessian Minister for Economic Affairs personally engaged in discussions with municipal representatives, signaling high-level recognition of the project’s relevance. The practical tools and findings generated through the project will inform future advisory services of the State Energy Agency (LEA).DiscussionThe study demonstrates the significant impact of a transdisciplinary, trust-based approach to addressing the challenges of building modernization in smaller municipalities. The project successfully delivered both tangible tools and intangible benefits, advancing climate action in meaningful and sustainable ways. Among its key outputs were practical tools such as governance profiles, communication strategies, and process flowcharts, which provided municipalities with clear guidance on implementing building modernization measures. These deliverables not only addressed immediate municipal needs but also strengthened long-term capacity to manage and implement climate-friendly building practices by enhancing administrative and governance systems.Participants in the project came from diverse roles within municipal governments, reflecting Martin’s categorization of practitioners: technical experts who implement policies, managers who oversee implementation and communicate with political stakeholders, and politicians with decision-making authority15. In smaller municipalities, these roles were often combined, reflecting resource limitations. The participants brought extensive knowledge of their local contexts and challenges, particularly concerning building modernization. While many municipalities had pre-existing climate action measures, such as climate protection concepts and funding programs, the implementation of building modernization remained weak. The project specifically aimed to address this gap by fostering collaboration and co-producing solutions tailored to local needs.The collaborative, co-productive approach allowed participants to identify key challenges, prioritize areas for improvement, and develop actionable solutions. The workshops provided a setting in which local and experiential knowledge could be combined with scientific expertise and the experiences of peers from other municipalities. Through joint reflection and discussion, participants were able to translate specific challenges into concrete questions of how to act under their respective municipal conditions. In this process, transformation knowledge developed not simply through the provision of information, but through the joint exploration and testing of possible courses of action. Two working groups focused on distinct but complementary areas: funding and communication. The funding group developed guidelines for navigating funding processes, including applications, project execution, and governance-level completion. Meanwhile, the communication group analyzed administrative workflows, identified key stakeholders, and created resolutions to support advocacy for modernization goals within their municipalities. These efforts enabled participants to refine both their target knowledge – clarifying what outcomes were needed – and their transformation knowledge – developing practical methods to achieve those outcomes. The development of these practical methods was closely linked to the collaborative process: participants jointly reflected on existing administrative practices, exchanged experiences, and adapted the emerging solutions to their local contexts. The co-produced solutions were directly applicable to municipal governance, significantly enhancing participants’ ability to implement effective building modernization initiatives. The subsequent testing of these solutions in concrete municipal projects further supported this process by allowing participants to reflect on how the jointly developed approaches worked in practice and to adapt them where necessary. To ensure that the outcomes of the project are in line with the practitioners’ needs, the project team documented and reflected on the processes during the entire project duration. In addition to that, the transdisciplinary approach in the project was constantly being maintained by referring back to the developed transfer questions.A critical factor for the project’s success was the interdisciplinary collaboration between its partner institutions. The Institute for Housing and Environment and Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences contributed scientific and technical expertise on governance and modernization. The Schader-Stiftung complemented these efforts by fostering dialog and trust, developing innovative formats for workshop engagement, and serving as the primary point of contact for participants. The foundation’s ability to facilitate communication and collaboration played a vital role in maintaining participant engagement and ensuring the project’s transdisciplinary approach was effective. This combination of academic rigor and innovative communication strategies sets the project apart from other initiatives in the field.One of the project’s most significant achievements was the level of trust and mutual support it established among participants and the project team. Participants frequently shared their findings and drafts voluntarily, seeking feedback and enabling collective learning. Such exchanges contributed to transforming knowledge by allowing participants to compare their own experiences with those of peers, reflect on possible courses of action, and gain confidence in addressing similar challenges in their own municipalities. Municipal representatives also initiated bilateral and trilateral collaborations beyond the project’s formal framework, exchanging insights on specific methods and best practices. This sense of community empowered participants to navigate their challenges more confidently and fostered recognition that their struggles were shared by peers in similar contexts. Such voluntary engagement and collaboration underscored the project’s role as a multiplier, amplifying its impact beyond the immediate scope of its workshops. In this way, the project contributed to the emergence of a community of practice, in which municipal representatives shared experiences, developed joint strategies, and continued learning from one another beyond the formal project boundaries. The innovative and safer spaces that were fostered by the project team had a significant impact on the results of the project. The outcomes of the project show that the trusted environment that was created significantly enhanced the production of transformation knowledge and the implementation of climate action in the participating municipalities. The fostering of spaces such as these that differ significantly from the municipalities’ routines and offer environments that allow people in similar situations to think, process, and share complaints, but most importantly create answers to challenges in their work life, is highly productive. The paper shows that this approach of transdisciplinary research and collaboration can produce a variety of outcomes that concern the creation of transformation knowledge and its implementation.These findings also provide a more differentiated understanding of how co-production and innovative spaces can contribute to the development of transformation knowledge. In line with the literature on transdisciplinary research, the results show that transformation knowledge emerged through the combination of scientific expertise with the practical knowledge and experiences of municipal actors. At the same time, the findings suggest that the contribution of co-production lies not only in bringing different knowledge bases together, but in creating opportunities to jointly reflect on challenges, develop context-specific courses of action, and test these approaches in practice. In this respect, the findings refine the concept of innovative spaces introduced above: their value appears to derive not simply from being separate from everyday municipal routines, but from the combination of a protected setting, sustained exchange among peers, external facilitation, and opportunities to connect reflection with practical experimentation. These conditions supported participants in moving from identifying what needed to change towards exploring how change could be pursued within their specific administrative and political contexts. This supports the assumption in the transdisciplinary literature that sustained involvement of practitioners in solution development can strengthen their capacity to act and their ownership of the resulting solutions.The project also encountered challenges, particularly related to the limited time and personnel resources available to participating municipalities. These constraints occasionally affected participants’ ability to prepare for workshops or complete tasks between sessions. To mitigate this, the project team structured activities to minimize additional workload and offered flexibility for participants to pause or rejoin as needed. Despite these limitations, the high level of engagement demonstrated by most participants reflected their recognition of the project’s value and the practical relevance of its outcomes. In addition to these practical constraints, the research process itself was influenced by the transdisciplinary approach. The researchers were not external observers but actively involved as facilitators, co-creators, and analysts. This dual role required continuous reflection on their own positioning and its potential impact on interactions and interpretations. Such methodological limitations are inherent to transdisciplinary research and underline the importance of reflexivity and transparent documentation. The project evaluation further confirmed that the balance between scientific rigor and practical engagement was successfully managed, reinforcing the effectiveness of this transdisciplinary approach.Ultimately, the project’s lasting impact lies not only in the tangible outputs it produced but also in the intangible benefits it fostered. By creating a space where participants felt safe sharing challenges and collaboratively developing solutions, the project empowered municipal agents to take actionable steps in addressing building modernization issues. The relationships and trust cultivated during the project have already led to the implementation of co-produced solutions in municipal practices, transforming local approaches to building modernization. This trust-based, transdisciplinary model offers a replicable framework for municipalities facing similar challenges, demonstrating that systemic barriers can be overcome through collaboration, practical innovation, and sustained engagement.MethodsResearch framework and case studyThe results and findings described above are based on a transdisciplinary research project on the governance of building modernization in 12 small and medium-sized municipalities throughout Hesse, Germany. To be able to generate transformation knowledge in the context of climate action for sustainable building modernizations in smaller municipalities, we developed and utilized a transdisciplinary framework. This made it possible to deal with issues that are a priority for the municipal stakeholders and to generate a sense of ownership for the solutions developed among the participating municipalities. The three-phase model of Lang et al. in the further developed version of Kleihauer (refer to Figs. 1, 2) was applied here14,19.Fig. 2: The phases of the td project.Full size imageThis figure shows the described three main phases and the subphases of the transdisciplinary research framework. Adopted and adapted from Kleihauer19.To succeed, the phases of the td project were transferred into a three-stage workshop concept, which was developed in intensive cooperation between the three project partners involved: the Institut Wohnen und Umwelt (Institute for Housing and Environment) as an expert in building modernization, the Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences as an established transdisciplinary knowledge institution, and the Schader-Stiftung as a foundation with the aim of promoting communication and cooperation between the social sciences and practice40. The scientific project team comprised various disciplines, from political science and spatial planning with expertise in urban development, urban management, and governance to cultural studies with experience in process design and facilitation, to lawyers and engineers with legal and technical knowledge of building modernization. This combination of expertise made it possible to address the needs of the participating municipalities regarding both the technical and legal aspects of building modernization, while also effectively designing and facilitating the complex co-creative process with its demanding requirements for process planning and facilitation.The practitioners involved brought a wide variety of backgrounds, skills, and design options to the project. These ranged from less experienced to very experienced administrative staff in various positions in local government, from consultants working across local authorities to mayors who were actively involved in the td project.The three-stage workshop concept (see Fig. 3) operationalized the project phases A1 (joint problem framing), B1 (developing solutions), and B2 (testing solutions) with a series of interactive workshops providing the spaces needed to co-produce and test solutions with the selected municipalities (see Table 1). The workshops, typically lasting three to four hours, involved direct participation from the municipal representatives and were facilitated by the project team. Custom dialog formats were developed for these workshops to foster discussions aimed at identifying and agreeing on the challenges and developing solutions that overcome common barriers, ultimately leading to accelerated and improved management of building modernization.Fig. 3: Transdisciplinary spaces for co-production: implementation across the project phases.Full size imageThe figure illustrates how the three-phase framework was implemented through different formats and activities across the project.Table 1 Structured overview of dialog formats appliedFull size tableDialog formats appliedProject Kick-off Event (Phase A0): The kick-off event in March 2023 brought together the selected municipalities for the first time, along with various stakeholders involved in building modernization and transdisciplinary research. The event aimed to inform participants about the project and its upcoming phases while establishing an initial foundation of trust. From the beginning, fostering a supportive environment for open exchange between the municipalities was a priority. To encourage candid discussions, the group adopted the “Chatham House Rule,” meaning that statements could be shared in general terms but without attributing them to specific individuals35.The physical setup of the kick-off event – a central circle of chairs for the municipal representatives, surrounded by an outer circle for invited stakeholders and the project team (see Fig. 4) – immediately emphasized the core focus of the project: the participating municipalities, their needs, and their input.Fig. 4: Physical setup of the kick-off event.Full size imageThe participating municipalities at the center (“inner circle”) of the discussion, with other participants positioned in the second row (“outer circle”) as contributors.While the outer circle participants were occasionally invited to contribute, their primary role was that of observers and listeners. Key questions such as “What challenges related to building modernization of municipal properties are already identifiable?” and “What are the expectations for the project?” were discussed. The responses were visualized and documented in real-time on pinboards and sticky notes, later organized and shared digitally with all participants. This process provided an initial snapshot of the status of building modernization in the municipalities as of spring 2023, highlighting both existing challenges and potential solutions. It quickly became apparent that challenges outweighed solutions and that many municipalities faced similar obstacles. This shared understanding of the issues allowed the project team to tailor the subsequent workshops to the specific needs of municipal representatives.Due to the number of municipalities involved and their stakeholders, but above all due to the large distances between the case municipalities from all over the state of Hesse, two groups (North and South) were formed. The workshops were thus organized in two parallel strands and held at two different locations in order to reduce the need for practitioners to travel. In addition to the reduction in travel times, another benefit of the split was that it kept the groups small, which promoted intensive mutual familiarization and the building of trust. The exchange with the other project municipalities was ensured on the one hand by the openness of the group membership and on the other hand by the continuous reporting from the other workshop groups' proceedings.Workshop #1 (Phase A1): The first workshop following the kick-off event served to deepen the joint problem understanding and to collaboratively draft transfer questions with the municipal representatives. Transfer questions aim to bring together the practical knowledge of the actors and scientific findings from a specific area in order to jointly develop solutions. It was crucial to create a trusting and safe discussion space that allowed participants to openly address sensitive issues such as structural problems, lack of resources, limited mandates, or even resistance from superiors or uninformed mayors. The starting point for understanding these challenges and expressing transfer questions was the input provided by the municipalities during the kick-off event.The first workshop began with an ice-breaker exercise to help participants get acquainted and build trust between the municipality representatives and the project team. This exercise was set up as a game of “Bingo” that was concerned with the topic of building modernization. The participants were engaged in getting to know each other while already discussing the topics at hand. Additionally, the exercise further underscored the tone for the project: it engages with the participants in a different way than might usually be the case. This was followed by an interactive exchange on building modernization, prompting participants to reflect not only on the measures already implemented but also to identify who – whether individuals, organizations, or institutions – is responsible for building modernization and who is already actively engaged in these efforts in their own municipalities. Each municipality worked on a pinboard, supported by members of the project team. In the final session, participants prioritized the challenges already identified at the kick-off event, now elaborated in greater detail. Defining these specific challenges and assessing which ones required the most attention was crucial for the project’s progression. The first workshop also initiated a period of work between the workshops. As a ‘homework’ task, the participants were asked to further reflect on the challenges identified and prioritized during the workshop, consider whether further challenges needed to be addressed, and reassess the priorities they had assigned. This provided the basis for the subsequent development of actionable change ideas in Phase A2. The project team supported this process between the workshops and used the results of this work as a basis for further developing the transfer questions for the subsequent workshops.Workshops #2 (Phase A2/B1): Workshop #2 acted as a bridge from Phase A2 to Phase B1. The focus of this workshop was on the transfer questions drafted by the scientific project team since the kick-off event. To enhance clarity and accessibility for practitioners, these questions were framed as ‘working questions’. Through a collaborative process, they were thoroughly discussed, refined, and developed further.Workshops 3-4 (Phase B1): In the following project phase B1, the practitioners developed solutions for the challenges of building modernization that they had identified in the previous workshops. The main emphasis here was on the transfer (‘working’) questions that the project team had drawn up based on the former input. These served as a basis for the participating municipalities to decide how to proceed with the content of the project. The questions were presented by the project team in workshop #2 and put up for discussion. This gave the participants the opportunity to deal with the aspects and jointly determine which ones were most relevant to them. Both the South and North groups came to the conclusion that topics from the areas of (a) “funding & financing” and (b) “information, advice” as well as “adapting the administrative structure” were of particular relevance. As a result, two substantive working groups on (a) “funding” and (b) “communication” were formed in the workshops to develop solutions in greater depth.These two working groups played a key role in shaping the content of the subsequent workshops. Under the guidance of the project team, the groups on funding and on communication developed targeted solutions to address the challenges encountered in building modernization within these areas. Both groups worked independently but were continuously supported by the project team. The project team acted as moderators, summarizing the ideas brought forward and steering discussions in a focused manner. Together, the participants identified solutions that are particularly practical and beneficial for implementation in everyday municipal operations.Workshops #5-7 (Phase B2): Phase B2 marked the transition to the practical testing of the previously developed solutions. Under the guidance of the project team, the participating municipalities tested the results of the previous work phase in their local context. Each municipality selected a specific project to test the applicability and potential of the proposed solutions. Municipalities that did not currently run a suitable building modernization project either back-tested already completed projects or planned possible future initiatives in which the solutions could be implemented from the outset.During the three workshops held for each group (North and South) in phase B2, the municipalities were given regular opportunities to exchange updates on their testing phases. These gatherings fostered collaboration by allowing participants to share progress, address challenges, and seek advice from both the project team and other municipalities. The workshops were thoughtfully designed to balance input from the participating municipalities with targeted input from the project team on several issues concerning building modernizations. Key inputs included guidance on digital tools to streamline the modernization process and opportunities to connect with external institutions that could assist in municipal operations. For several inputs from the municipalities, the participants were tasked in advance with preparing their updates with the help of PowerPoint slides. This approach supported those who felt uncertain about presenting their progress, while others spoke more freely. The workshops were moderated in such a way that there was enough room to hold space for the participants’ experiences during their trial phase and for the project team to react and advise on issues that came up in the presentations. In this phase, the municipal representatives were tasked with testing the co-created solutions independently in their own contexts and reporting on their findings in the workshops. This turn empowered municipalities to take ownership of the process while retaining access to project team support for any questions or challenges that arose.The final workshops for the South and North groups were held in the summer of 2024, about approximately six months before the project’s closing event in January 2025. These workshops aimed to prepare the participating municipalities for the final project phase, during which no further workshops would be held. The sessions focused on equipping municipalities to continue the testing phase independently, without the regular check-ins that had characterized earlier phases. At the same time, the workshops provided space for a first round of feedback on the project itself. This feedback was gathered at a basic level in order to gain an early sense of how the project was being perceived, without implying that the active part of the project was over. The project team made sure to communicate that despite the completion of the workshop phases, there was still a way to get in touch if there were any questions or concerns. This marked the end of the workshop part of the project.In between the Workshops: While the workshops, as described above, involved intensive group work on solutions and plenty of room for personal and inter-municipal exchange, the organization of the stages between the workshops was also crucial for the progress of the project: Through regular ‘homework’, the participants were required to stay engaged with the project and the work steps. Between the workshops, the project team consistently checked with the municipal agents, staying in touch via phone, video calls, email, or site visits in order to keep the project and its agenda in the minds of the practitioners and also to signal that the team was there for them. Throughout the project, these interactions and observations of the collaborative process were documented in an ongoing project log. The project team used this documentation to reflect on the process and to keep the research questions in view throughout the project, including during regular team meetings on a weekly basis. The observations and process documentation were used to contextualize and interpret the findings but were not subject to a separate systematic analysis. The empirical evaluation reported in this paper was based on the standardized questionnaire and the subsequent semi-structured interviews.Project Evaluation and Data Analysis: To assess the project’s effectiveness, outcomes, and participants’ experiences, the evaluation was conducted in two stages. First, a standardized and anonymous questionnaire was administered via Particify to all 12 participating municipalities. Representatives of 10 municipalities completed the questionnaire. The questionnaire addressed participants’ perceptions of the project process and its different facilitation formats, including the usefulness of in-person and online meetings, the working groups, tasks conducted between the workshop phases, and bilateral discussions with the project team. It also addressed participants’ assessments of the project outputs and their usefulness for municipal practice. In a second step, follow-up semi-structured personal interviews were conducted to explore participants’ perspectives in greater depth, clarify and elaborate on issues raised in the questionnaire, and provide an opportunity to address specific aspects of the project in more detail. All 12 participating municipalities were invited to an interview; six municipalities participated. The approximately one-hour interviews were conducted via videoconference by two researchers from the project team, recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using qualitative content analysis following Mayring41. The analysis combined a deductive and an inductive approach: findings from the standardized questionnaire were used to form the initial thematic categories for the interviews, which were then complemented by inductively derived categories emerging from the interview material. The interview guide covered three main thematic areas: (1) the usefulness and practical applicability of the project outputs and the effects of the project on participants’ knowledge, understanding, and ability to act; (2) participants’ experiences of the project process, including the different roles of the project team, collaboration on an equal footing, workshop formats and atmosphere, and the relevance of the agreed Chatham House Rules; and (3) participants’ expectations, key moments, perceived potential for improvement, and willingness to engage in similar collaborative processes in the future.Researcher positionality and practitioner involvement: During the course of the project and the preparation of this paper, one of the co-authors assumed an intermediary role between the “traditional” scientific community and municipal stakeholders. This facilitative role supported the dialog between research and practice and contributed to the interpretation of the empirical findings. Municipal practitioners were not directly involved in the analysis or writing of the paper; their perspectives were incorporated through the questionnaire, interviews, project observations, and ongoing exchange during the project. The collaboration among the authors continues the project’s transdisciplinary orientation, as the author team remained in continuous exchange across differing perspectives on the subject matter throughout the interpretation and writing process. This continued engagement with different perspectives is also reflected in related publications emerging from the project, including the paper by Schoenefeld and Wasmer on the actors involved in building modernization34.Ethical considerations and informed consentThe empirical data were collected as part of a project evaluation that served both research purposes and the internal and applied evaluation of the project. Participants in the survey and interviews were informed about the purpose of the data collection, the intended use of the data, including scientific use, and the principles of confidentiality and anonymization. Participation was voluntary and based on informed consent. No formal ethical approval was obtained from an ethics committee or institutional review board. All data were processed and reported in a way that prevents the identification of individual participants. No names or other directly identifying information are reported, and no verbatim quotations from interviews or other participant contributions are used. Project events were conducted under the Chatham House Rule, which was agreed upon with all participants.

Data availability
              
              Some of the data featured in this publication are derived from internal project documentation, such as facilitation plans, workshop minutes, the municipality profiles, and email exchanges between the foundation and municipal representatives. The datasets generated and analyzed during the study are not publicly available because they contain information collected from project participants under conditions of confidentiality and anonymization (Chatham House Rules). Making the underlying individual-level data publicly available could compromise the confidentiality agreed with participants. Aggregated findings and other non-identifying materials relevant to the study are presented in the article. Some of this data can be shared on request.
